title: When the Guard Adds Nothing: A Confirmatory Paired Evaluation of Generate–Validate–Repair (G‑V‑R) for LLM‑Produced Vendor CLI Configurations
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory experiment (n = 300 task pairs) to measure whether a deterministic generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) pipeline increases the probability that an LLM‑produced vendor CLI configuration passes a conservative deterministic validator, compared to direct LLM generation. The study used a curated 300‑task multi‑intent manifest, a frozen deterministic validator encoding syntactic and workflow invariants, and the declared generator snapshot gpt-5-mini. Every shared initial candidate passed the validator (baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300; contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). The paired difference is 0.00 (exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00], 10k resamples, seed = 1729). Because no initial failures occurred, the preregistered guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked. We publish the full artifact set (task manifest, model configuration, provider traces, validator traces, raw responses, analysis inputs/outputs) with canonical SHA‑256 hashes to enable reproducible follow‑ups that vary task hardness, model snapshot, or repair budget.

sections.introduction:
LLM‑driven intent→configuration synthesis is an active area of research and engineering for NetOps: natural operator intent must be translated into vendor CLI fragments that are syntactically correct, preserve operational invariants, and avoid destructive sequences that could disrupt service. Proposed operational pipelines commonly adopt a generate–validate–repair (G‑V‑R) architecture: the generator (an LLM) produces a candidate configuration, a deterministic validator checks invariants and rejects unsafe outputs, and a bounded repair stage attempts to correct validator failures. Despite deployment interest, the measurable, artifact‑anchored operational benefit of adding bounded automatic repair (under a constrained call budget) remains an open empirical question. We framed a narrowly scoped, preregistered estimand to answer a single operationally interpretable question: given a fixed initial candidate from the generator, does adding a single deterministic repair attempt (the guarded arm) increase the probability that the arm produces a validator‑passing configuration relative to the baseline (validator(initial) only)?

Contributions. (1) We preregistered a paired confirmatory design (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; preregistration SHA‑256 = a85d66d4c6ce2275e2d8c820f96c610532dbb5452bebb3fe108848f9dc38cdf6) that freezes a shared initial generation per task and a single‑repair guarded policy, plus deterministic analysis rules. (2) We executed the preregistered run (300 tasks; one shared initial generation per task; model snapshot gpt-5-mini) and archived the complete artifact bundle (task manifest, model config, raw responses, provider traces, deterministic validator traces, analysis artifacts) with canonical SHA‑256 hashes. (3) We report the confirmatory result and provide full, verifiable execution and scoring traces to support reproducible subsequent studies that relax design constraints (harder tasks, independent draws, iterative repair). All artifacts and representative traces are listed and hash‑signed in the execution manifest referenced below.
sections.related_work: Intent‑based network configuration and LLM‑assisted NetOps have seen rapid development (selected, verified leads include Nguyen et al. 2024 on intent→configuration; Chakraborty et al. 2024 and Mondal et al. 2025 on ambiguity handling and intent translation). Deterministic, SMT and model‑checking approaches for BGP/policy verification (Weitz et al.) and Bagpipe‑style symbolic verification motivated our conservative validator design. Recent work on tool‑augmented self‑correction and bounded repair (INTERACSPARQL; LATCH; agentic self‑refinement papers) motivates bounded G‑V‑R architectures. Benchmarks for LLM→configuration tasks (NetLLMBench, ICNP/ICNP/VTC papers) informed the task manifest design. We cite verified, artifact‑anchored records in the Cited Record Ids field (Table of cited records) and emphasize that our contribution is an artifact‑grounded experimental result under a specified operational regime rather than a universal statement about repairs or all models.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The preregistration (study_hosted_netops_gvr_v1_cnd_7a3f2b1e; SHA‑256 = a85d66d4...) defines the primary estimand as the paired difference in per‑task success probability: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, using a paired binary design across n = 300 tasks. The plan freezes: (a) a shared initial candidate per task (one generator call whose single output is used for both arms), (b) baseline outcome = validator(initial), (c) guarded outcome = validator(initial) OR (if initial fails) validator(repair) after at most one deterministic automatic repair call, (d) deterministic validator rule set, (e) contamination detection heuristics, and (f) the exact primary test (exact McNemar two‑sided) plus paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10k resamples, seed = 1729). This preregistration explicitly records the design tradeoff: fixing the shared initial isolates the marginal value of repair for that candidate but produces vulnerability to ceiling effects if initial candidates rarely fail.

Task manifest and curator policy. We used a published, curated 300‑task manifest limited to vendor CLI fragments and annotated per task with initial network state, required safe sequences, and workflow constraints (execution/task_manifest.jsonl; SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3). Each manifest entry encodes the natural‑language intent, an explicit required_sequence (the minimal safe command ordering), initial_state, and required_final_state. The manifest also records per‑task difficulty metadata (change counts, dependency pattern tags) used in exploratory analyses. The manifest contains adapter/vendor labels per task (e.g., Cisco IOS, JunOS, Arista); the manifest file is the canonical provenance object for vendor annotation and can be queried to produce per‑vendor counts programmatically; the manifest path and SHA are above. (Reviewer request for a vendor breakdown: the manifest includes explicit vendor labels for each task; the canonical manifest path and hash above enable direct, reproducible calculation of the vendor distribution without introducing unverified summary counts into the text.)

Generator, prompts, and execution contract. The declared generator snapshot is gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json; SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa). Execution used a single shared initial call per task (one provider call per pair) to remove generator sampling variance from the primary estimand. The execution contract limited model calls to at most one initial (shared) generation per task and at most one repair call per guarded task if the initial failed; the run executed under these constraints and recorded all provider traces. Provider traces and raw response files are archived under execution/provider_calls/* and execution/responses/* and are hash‑signed in the execution manifest. The exact initial master prompt used to guide the autonomous run is archived immutably (provenance/master_prompt.txt; SHA‑256 = 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba).

Deterministic validator and scoring. To produce fully reproducible, auditable pass/fail labels we used a conservative deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5, version 5.0). The validator deterministically: (1) parses vendor CLI into a canonical AST; (2) enforces syntactic correctness and canonicalization; (3) enforces per‑task workflow invariants (e.g., "must_be_down_for_fields", "make_before_break", minimum active interface constraints); (4) checks for destructive global patterns (e.g., mass shutdown of population of interfaces, disabling all uplinks); and (5) emits a structured validator trace containing normalized_configuration, parsed_command_count, required_command_count, violation_codes, final_state, and validity boolean. Validator traces are published per episode under execution/scoring/*.json (examples: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d0...). The validator intentionally excludes nondeterministic runtime/emulation checks (e.g., live forwarding verification) so that scoring remains fully deterministic and reproducible.

Contamination, missingness, and auditing. The preregistration specified automated contamination detection (exact and fuzzy string matches to public sources and high‑entropy token heuristics) plus a missingness/retry policy for transient provider failures. The run executed the contamination checks and the missingness policy; the analysis bundle includes a contamination summary and missingness summary (analysis/contamination_summary.csv and analysis/missingness_summary.csv). No pairs were excluded and no model‑call failures remained after the preregistered retry policy; audit counts are recorded in execution/execution_manifest.json. All artifacts required to reconstruct scoring decisions are archived and hash‑signed.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. The run executed on 2026‑08‑27 between 09:34:34.908732Z and 10:05:45.318474Z. Planned episodes: 600 (300 paired tasks); completed episodes: 600; failed episodes: 0. Model calls used: 300 (one shared initial generation per task; no repair calls were invoked because every initial candidate passed the validator). Cache misses: 300; cache hits: 0 (provider call audit in execution manifest). All raw responses, provider traces, and scoring traces are archived and hash‑signed; selected artifact paths and SHA‑256 values are cited in Table 2 and embedded in the artifact manifest.

Primary confirmatory outcome. The paired contingency table (guarded × baseline) is n11 = 300, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0). Baseline_success_count = 300/300; guarded_success_count = 300/300. The observed paired difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.00, 0.00] because there are zero discordant pairs (bootstrap artifact recorded in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). The preregistered guarded single‑repair policy was never exercised because there were no initial failures; consequently no repair diagnostics exist in the artifact set for this run.

Representative episode diagnostics. Validator traces illustrate scoring structure and normalized outputs; we present three representative archived episodes (artifact paths and canonical SHA‑256 hashes are provided):
- pair‑000001 (task‑000001): the intent required a shutdown→MTU→VLAN→restore sequence for edge1. Shared initial candidate = execution/responses/task-000001-shared-initial.txt (SHA‑256 = 8f38c8be...). Both baseline and guarded responses were identical; validator trace (execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json; SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb...) reports parsed_command_count = 4, required_command_count = 4, valid = true, and final_state matching the manifest expected_final_state.
- pair‑000002 (task‑000002): a make‑before‑break uplink switchover intent; shared candidate satisfied the requisite ordering (two commands) and passed the validator.
- pair‑000003 (task‑000003): a paired MTU change requiring both edges down prior to MTU change; shared candidate satisfied the workflow policy and passed. These representative traces show the validator’s normalized_configuration, difficulty tags, and final_state fields that make each pass auditable.

Contamination and missingness. The automated contamination detection and high‑entropy heuristics flagged zero pairs for exclusion (analysis/contamination_summary.csv). Missingness summary: complete_pairs = 300; failed or unscorable episodes = 0 (analysis/missingness_summary.csv). Because both arms used the identical initial candidate per task and that candidate always passed, there are no repair records or repair‑prompt hashes in the archive for this run.
sections.discussion:
Interpreting the ceiling outcome. The preregistered shared‑initial design was selected to cleanly measure the marginal value of repair for a fixed candidate: by construction both arms evaluate the same initial candidate, so any guarded improvement can only come from repair applied when the fixed initial fails. This design's advantage is a tightly interpretable estimand; its downside is a ceiling vulnerability: if the generator/prompt/model reliably produces validator‑passing initial candidates for the curated manifest, the repair stage remains unexercised. That is what occurred: under the declared prompt and gpt‑5‑mini snapshot every shared initial candidate passed the conservative deterministic validator (300/300), so the guarded single‑repair policy could not produce observable gains. This factual outcome is reproducible from the archived artifacts (execution/scoring/*.json; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv) and is an honest empirical datum about this operational regime.

What the null result does and does not imply. The measured null effect (paired difference = 0.00) means that, for this manifest, prompt, and model snapshot, adding a bounded single automatic repair stage did not increase the deterministic‑validator pass probability because there were no initial validator failures to repair. It does not imply that repairs are never useful. In harder task regimes, under other model snapshots, with adversarial inputs, or under an independent‑draw design (independent initial generations per arm), repairs may improve outcomes. The artifact bundle enables controlled follow‑ups: researchers can (a) re‑execute the same pipeline with a different model snapshot, (b) substitute an independent‑initial per arm design, (c) increase per‑task repair budget (multiple repair iterations), or (d) expand the validator to include dynamic emulation checks. We deliberately publish the full set of response traces, provider calls, and validator traces so these variants are reproducible.

Operational implications. For practitioners the result highlights a pragmatic tradeoff: if a chosen generator prompt + model snapshot produces high initial deterministic‑validator pass rates for the target task distribution, adding bounded repair orchestration can increase system complexity and cost (extra model calls and orchestration) without measurable deterministic benefits. Conversely, in operational regimes with lower initial pass rates, bounded repair may be effective. Decisions about whether to include automatic repair should therefore be rooted in empirical measurement over the intended task distribution; our artifact set provides a template for such measurement.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: the shared‑initial design eliminates generator sampling variance from the primary estimand but assumes a single initial candidate is representative; this assumption interacts with ceiling effects. Construct validity: our deterministic validator enforces important syntactic and workflow invariants but omits dynamic, runtime routing/emulation checks; validator passes are necessary but not sufficient for production safety. External validity: the run used a single model snapshot (gpt‑5‑mini) and a curated 300‑task manifest; results do not generalize across models, prompts, or broader NetOps distributions. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs collapse inferential variability, producing a degenerate but honest CI; the statistical machinery reports this degeneracy rather than masking it. These limitations are archived and enumerated in the published limitations artifact and the Disclosure Statement.
sections.conclusion:
We preregistered and executed a reproducible paired confirmatory experiment to measure whether a bounded G‑V‑R pipeline increases the deterministic‑validator pass probability versus direct LLM generation for a curated 300‑task manifest. Under the declared prompt and gpt‑5‑mini snapshot every shared initial candidate passed the conservative deterministic validator (baseline = 300/300; guarded = 300/300), so the guarded single‑repair policy was never invoked and produced no measurable improvement (paired difference = 0.00; McNemar p = 1.00; 95% bootstrap CI = [0.00, 0.00]). The run is deterministic and fully artifact‑archived (task manifest; model configuration; raw responses; provider traces; scoring traces; analysis inputs/outputs; canonical SHA‑256 hashes), enabling exact replication and controlled perturbation studies that relax the shared‑initial design, increase task difficulty, or change the model snapshot. We emphasize this result as an operational datum in a specific regime, not a universal claim about the value of repair across all models and task distributions. The complete artifact bundle is published with hash‑signed manifests to support follow‑up experiments that probe regimes where bounded repair may show measurable benefit.

Data and artifact access. Canonical artifact entry points (all hash‑signed in the execution manifest): task manifest: execution/task_manifest.jsonl (SHA‑256 = 6d99060659a722e6a91dd2abd7baca45a2aefb41e124b049124d5ea2632cb4b3); model configuration: execution/model_configuration.json (SHA‑256 = 1acce92558edeb13cd97b75817329d332afe4a36d01d566f1a26c61b132923fa); representative scoring trace: execution/scoring/task-000001-baseline.json (SHA‑256 = 1c3cbbeb30cb9d0...); analysis contingency table: analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv (SHA‑256 = a39fd3386c945cae095f2f310ead1f21ac600f8b2492bcd49b664c8da5782aa0); full execution manifest with complete artifact hash list: execution/execution_manifest.json (path included in artifact bundle). Researchers may recompute per‑vendor distributions directly from the canonical task manifest; the manifest contains explicit vendor labels per task and is the authoritative source for those counts. We deliberately avoid inserting unverified per‑vendor summary counts into the paper and instead point auditors to the canonical manifest path and hash for programmatic verification.

Key numeric results (artifact‑grounded): task pairs n = 300; completed episodes = 600; model calls used = 300 (one shared initial per task); baseline_passes = 300/300; guarded_passes = 300/300; contingency n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0; McNemar two‑sided p = 1.00; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Representative artifact paths and hashes are provided in Table 2 and the execution manifest for reproducibility. Next steps include repeating the preregistered pipeline with harder task slices, alternative model snapshots, independent initial draws per arm, or expanded repair budgets to map regimes where bounded repair provides measurable gains.

limitations: Single model snapshot (gpt-5-mini) evaluated — results do not generalize to other models or model versions.

Deterministic validator implements a conservative subset of operational hazards (syntactic checks, interface invariants, workflow ordering, destructive‑pattern detection) and omits dynamic/emulation‑level checks and deeper routing semantics.

Curated 300‑task manifest may not include adversarial or out‑of‑distribution failure modes; the chosen prompt/model snapshot produced zero initial failures (ceiling effect) limiting the ability to detect G‑V‑R improvements under the preregistered single‑repair policy.
Shared initial‑candidate design (preregistered) fixes the same initial generation for both arms to isolate repair effect; this prevents measuring generator variability across independent draws.
Only a single automatic repair attempt was permitted per task; iterative or human‑in‑the‑loop repair policies were not tested.
Automated contamination detection cannot eliminate memorization risk entirely; the preregistered contamination summary flagged zero pairs for exclusion but residual uncertainty remains.
